steps.ask: What equation do you solve to find where the two graphs meet?
steps.title: Find where the two graphs cross

lines.text: $f(x) = g(x)$ where the graphs meet, at $x = \hl{1}{-1}$ and $x = \hl{1}{2}$.

steps.ask: Between the crossing points, which graph is higher? Which graph is higher outside them?
steps.title: Find where f(x) is less than g(x)

lines.text: Between $x = \hl{1}{-1}$ and $x = \hl{1}{2}$ the graph of $f$ is below the graph of $g$.
Outside that range $f$ is above $g$. Do not include the endpoints, because there $f(x) = g(x)$.

problems.note: Problem 1 asked for the region where $f(x) < g(x)$. This asks only for the points where $f(x) = g(x)$, so the region step is dropped and a check step is added: substitute each x-value into both functions. Reading the crossings is the same.

steps.ask: Which points on the graph of m lie on the x-axis?
steps.title: Find where m(x) = 0

lines.text: $m(x) = 0$ where the graph of $m$ meets the $x$-axis.

steps.ask: Where do the graphs of k and m meet? Which x-values belong to those points?
steps.title: Find where the two graphs cross

lines.text: The graphs of $k$ and $m$ cross at $x = \hl{1}{2}$ and $x = \hl{1}{3.5}$.

steps.ask: Between the two crossing points, which graph is higher? Where is k(x) below m(x)?

steps.ask: How far must A move horizontally and vertically to reach C?
steps.title: Find the translation that maps A onto C

steps.ask: Where does the maximum point end up after the same move?
steps.title: Apply the translation to the maximum point (2.177, 4.529)

lines.text: Use the maximum height from part (i); the translation moves every point of the curve the same way.

problems.note: The move is now given as g(x − 4) − 2 instead of worked out from two points, and it is applied to three points instead of one. The method is the same: shift each point. A new step also shifts the domain.

steps.ask: Which way does x − 4 move the graph, and by how much?
steps.title: Horizontal shift: g(x − 4) moves the graph right 4

lines.text: Replacing $x$ by $x - 4$ shifts every point 4 units right, so $(x, y)$ becomes $(x + 4, y)$.

steps.ask: What must x − 4 lie between, and what does that give for x?
steps.title: Find the new domain

lines.text: $g$ needs its input between $-1$ and $3$.

steps.ask: Where does each point go after the 2 is subtracted?
steps.title: Vertical shift: subtracting 2 moves the graph down 2

lines.text: Every point then drops 2 units, so $(x, y)$ becomes $(x + 4, y - 2)$.

problems.note: Two separate moves are applied to the same three points, first a vertical shift and then a horizontal one, and the domain is found for the horizontal move. It is still shifting points, so the method is the same.

steps.ask: After subtracting 2, which coordinate of each point changes?
steps.title: (i) g(x) − 2 moves the graph down 2

lines.text: Subtracting 2 from the output lowers every point by 2; the domain stays $-2 \le x \le 2$.

steps.ask: Where does each point go when x is replaced by x + 3? Which way does it move?
steps.title: (ii) g(x + 3) moves the graph left 3

lines.text: Adding 3 to the input shifts every point 3 units left.

steps.ask: What must x + 3 lie between for g to accept it, and what does that give for x?
steps.title: Find the domain of g(x + 3)

lines.text: $g$ needs its input between $-2$ and $2$.

problems.final: \text{(i) } g(x) - 2 \text{ is } g(x) \text{ down 2; (ii) } g(x+3) \text{ is } g(x) \text{ left 3}
